title: If the twin is optimistic, how often does a rollout test certify a policy that is not safe?
lede: exact: a twin that fails 10% less often than reality lifts the chance of certifying a 5%-failure policy from 0.049 to 0.087 (fixed test, 1% vs 5%), 20% less often to 0.147, and guarding against a 1.5x optimism costs 2.2 times the rollouts
summary: Exact dynamic-programming study (no sampling) of what a constant twin-to-real optimism ratio does to a 5%-error rollout certificate, for the fixed binomial test and Wald’s sequential test. For 1% vs 5% (fixed test: 181 rollouts) the chance of certifying a policy whose real failure rate is 5% rises from 0.049 to 0.087 when the twin fails 10% less often, 0.147 at 20% less and 0.526 at 50% less; the sequential test is within 0.02 of it, so neither is more robust. It doubles to 10% at a ratio of 0.87 (0.93 for the narrower 5% vs 10% and 10% vs 20% pairs, where a 30% optimistic twin certifies more often than not). Guarding against optimism up to R by testing p0/R costs 1.27 times the rollouts at R = 1.1, 2.17 at 1.5 and 4.55 at 2 for 1% vs 5%, and cannot be done for the narrow pairs at R = 2. Four rate pairs, iid rollouts, a pure ratio bias that is an input, not measured from any real twin.
